articles.title: Religions, Vol. 17, Pages 1390: Martyrologization: Damaged Catholic Churches and the Making of Christian Suffering After Chile’s 2019 Social Uprising
articles.description: During the protests that began with Chile’s 2019 social uprising, attacks on Catholic churches reached a scale and intensity exceptional in Chilean political life, amid broader demands for social justice and institutional accountability. This article examines how selected damaged objects and sites came to bear witness to collective Christian suffering. Based on fieldwork, interviews, and documentary and audiovisual materials, it conceptualizes martyrologization as a selective socio-material process involving three operations: establishing evidentiary connections between material forms and violent events, interpreting damage within Christian temporalities of suffering, and extending its significance to wider Christian collectives. Catholic and civil society actors interpreted the attacks in divergent ways, including sacrilege, heritage loss, and the Church’s own responsibility. Within this contested field, Catholic media and devotional practices associated with international Catholic charity Aid to the Church in Need (ACN) linked damaged objects and sites to transnational narratives of the persecuted Church. These articulations emerged without human martyrs associated with the attacks and despite ACN’s classification of Chile as falling below its thresholds for discrimination and persecution. Bringing studies of political iconoclasm into dialogue with material religion, the article shows how claims of collective Christian vulnerability take shape amid disputes over Catholic public authority.
